alternative: Order the initialisation explicitly instead: an init/create function that initialises the payload first and hands a pointer to it to the initialiser of the dependent block, with the payload declared as the first member of the aggregate so the address relation is stable. C has no base subobjects to relocate, so there is no helper class to introduce - the ordering is simply the order of the statements you write.
idiom_name: explicit init order in a constructor function (no base subobjects to order)
implementation_notes: C has neither base classes nor a base-before-member rule: a struct is a sequence of members whose addresses increase in declaration order, and which of them is initialised first is decided by the initialiser list or by the init function you write. What replaces the classic structure is therefore the ordering itself - build the payload struct first and pass a pointer to it into the initialiser of the block that needs it, keeping the payload as the first member when the dependent block must know its address; nesting the dependent block inside the aggregate instead of deriving from it is the composition answer C always has. There is no helper type to introduce and nothing to encapsulate, and the classic form is never justified because the constraint the idiom removes does not exist.
pitfalls: The ordering guarantee is only as good as the constructor function: nothing in the type stops someone from initialising the dependent part first, and a designated initialiser may list members in any order it likes.
Storing a pointer to an embedded member (stream.buf = &s->buf) makes the object position-sensitive: copying or moving the struct leaves the pointer aiming at the old storage, with no diagnostic.
